question: Does this questionnaire measure what it claims to?

clark1995.cite: Clark & Watson (1995). Constructing validity: Basic issues in objective scale development. Psychological Assessment 7(3): 309–319.
clark1995.checked: every quote read word for word in the vault's text copy of the article (library No. 283) on 20 Nov 2026; page numbers are the journal's (the copy starts at p. 309); words broken across lines in the scan are joined

steps.title: Define the construct
steps.text: Write down exactly what the scale should capture, and how it relates to neighbouring ideas, before writing a single item.

quotes.text: A critical first step is to develop a precise and detailed conception of the target construct and its theoretical context.

steps.title: Write too many items
steps.text: Draft a broad pool of items, more than you will keep, covering the construct and its edges, each worded with care.

quotes.text: the content of the initial item pool should be overinclusive and item wording needs careful attention.

steps.title: Test widely
steps.text: Give the pool, with measures of related constructs, to a varied sample that spans the whole population the scale is for.

quotes.text: the item pool should be tested, along with variables that assess closely related constructs, on a heterogeneous sample representing the entire range of the target population.

steps.title: Keep one dimension
steps.text: Keep the items that measure one thing together, using factor analysis, not those that merely push internal consistency up.

quotes.text: in selecting scale items, the goal is unidimensionality rather than internal consistency; this means that virtually all interitem correlations should be moderate in magnitude.
Factor analysis can play a crucial role in ensuring the unidimensionality and discriminant validity of scales.

steps.title: Check the pattern
steps.text: The finished scale should correlate with what theory says it should, and not with what it should not.

quotes.text: a good measure will have a predicted convergent and discriminant correlational pattern

construct-validity.text: A primary goal of scale development is to create a valid measure of an underlying construct.

limits: The Maslach Burnout Inventory example on the card is not worked through here; its 1981 development paper has not been read for this page.
Test–retest reliability and the choice of response format, which Clark & Watson (1995) also discuss, are left out.
